lines: A buyer sends you a 1,200 dollar check for your 700 dollar bike and asks you to send back the extra 500. Two weeks later the check bounces, and you've lost 1,200 dollars.

Almost every scam uses the same four red flags. Pressure to act now. A strange way to pay, like gift cards, crypto, a wire, or a payment app to a stranger. Asking for a code or password. And an offer that's too good to be true.
With a fake check, the money shows up in your account within days, but finding out the check is fake can take weeks. When it bounces, the bank takes it all back.

Phishing is a fake text, email or call pretending to be your bank or another company you trust. Don't use its link or its number. Open your bank's app yourself, or call the number on the back of your card.
A real bank will never ask for the code it texts you. That code is the key to your account.
Payment apps work like cash. With people you don't know, use a credit card, where your fraud liability is capped at 50 dollars.
Identity theft is when someone opens accounts in your name. A credit freeze at all three bureaus is free and stops that. Use different passwords and turn on two-factor login.
If it happens, call your bank, change your passwords, freeze your credit, and report it at Identity Theft dot gov or Report Fraud dot F T C dot gov.
In the dark deep sea, the anglerfish dangles a glowing lure, and small fish swim right to it. A scam message is the lure. Before you swim toward the light, look for what's behind it.
